newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens to pick parliament, president.
newsitem.headline: Chechens to pick parliament, president.

text.p: Chechens on Monday choose a new president and parliament in controversial elections called after Russia abandoned its 21-month attempt to crush the Moslem region's independence drive.
Of 16 candidates for the five-year presidential term, only four are considered serious contenders.

Former Chechen guerrilla chief commander Aslan Maskhadov, 45, is still seen by most observers as the front runner, but he faces a strong challenge from Shamil Basayev, who grabbed world headlines in 1995 when he and 100 rebels took more than 1,000 hostages in a Russian hospital.
Wartime propaganda chief Movladi Udugov and acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev are the other main hopefuls.
A second round of voting will be held in three weeks if no candidate wins an overall majority. More than half the voters must turn up to make the polls valid.
A 63-member parliament will also be chosen.
Residents of the oil-rich region of about a million people can cast ballots from 7 a.m. (0400 GMT) to 8 p.m. (1600 GMT).
Refugees, concentrated in regions neighbouring Chechnya, can vote in polling stations near the borders of the Caucasus province.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is helping finance the organisation of the polls and is sending 60 observers.
Chechnya effectively exercised full independence from Russia from 1991 until December 1994 when Moscow sent troops to subdue separatism in the mountainous region.

But Moscow never established overall control of Chechnya during the military campaign, in which tens of thousands of people died. Disorganised and badly supported Russian troops faced stiff popular resistance.
On August 31 Moscow struck a peace deal with rebels under which it withdrew its forces from Chechnya and deferred any decision on Chechnya's status for five years.

But officials there, including the presidential candidates, make clear that they see independence as a fait accompli. Moscow is hoping to use ecomomic leverage to convince the region to remain part of the Russian Federation.
The pre-election campaign has clearly ruined the unity among separatist leaders welded by the hardships of the conflict.

Many Chechens have expressed dismay at the increasingly bitter campaign and clan elders, revered in this traditional society, have urged the main hopefuls to field a single candidate so as not to divide society.

Russia has hinted it may not recognise the election because it says polling places for refugees should be set up in Moscow and other Russian cities. The Chechens say refugee numbers are miniscule except in regions bordering their republic.

The vote has been overshadowed by the brutal murder of six foreign Red Cross workers in the town of Novy Atagi in December, the kidnapping of an orthodox priest and the disappearance of two Russian journalists.

The Chechen government says it has evidence linking Russian secret services to the Red Cross murders and that Moscow is bent on destabilising the region, thereby giving it an excuse to declare the poll invalid. Russia rejects the charges.
